slides.headline: Bees give directions to food by dancing. Here's the code.
Food close by? A round dance.
slides.body: A forager back from flowers near the hive circles on the comb, stirring nestmates to search. Beyond about 50 m, she waggle-dances instead.
slides.source: Nobel Prize press release (1973), von Frisch

slides.headline: The angle points the way
slides.body: On the vertical comb, 'straight up' stands for the sun. The waggle run's angle from vertical gives the food's direction relative to the sun.
slides.source: Nobel Prize press release (1973), von Frisch

slides.headline: The length tells the distance
slides.body: The longer each waggle run lasts, the farther away the food. Researchers calibrate it themselves, as the bee 'odometer' varies with landscape and strain.

slides.label: dances decoded over two years in one study
slides.body: Summer dances advertised food about 2.2 km away on average. In spring, it was about 0.5 km.

slides.headline: Radar proved the recruits listen
slides.body: Bees tracked by harmonic radar after watching a dance flew straight toward the feeder's area, then searched for the exact spot.

slides.headline: Save this for your next garden walk.
slides.body: Animal behaviour, decoded from the original research. Follow @claudes_plan101.
sources: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1973, press release (K. von Frisch)

caption:
The western honey bee (Apis mellifera) gives directions to food by dancing, encoding both direction and distance.

Karl von Frisch decoded it and shared the 1973 Nobel Prize for the work. Even when clouds hide the sun, bees can still read its position from polarised ultraviolet light. Decades later, radar tracking confirmed that recruits really do use the dance to fly to the food.

Swipe to learn the code. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Nobel Prize press release 1973; Couvillon et al. 2014, PLoS ONE; Riley et al. 2005, Nature.
